name: Torii Security Group Compact Combat Shotgun TSS-3 'Chorus'
description:
A five-chamber revolver shotgun in the Torii Security Group TSS-3 line. The cylinder is the action — there is no semi-automatic mechanism, no gas system, no magazine well. You load five 12-gauge shells into the cylinder, you fire five, you reload. The bird's-head grip is sharply recurved and stockless: the silhouette reads as an oversized revolver until you see the bore diameter, at which point it reads as a problem.

The TSS-3 is a Tier 3 commercial production model — available by order through Torii Security Group licensed distributors. The revolver-action configuration is the factory-default for the TSS-3; the bird's-head grip is a documented factory option, not a custom modification. What makes Kyle's unit Kyle's is the things he loads into it. A standard fixed-position speedloader carries five 12-gauge in a moon clip; Kyle keeps several pre-loaded in coat pockets, each labeled by load type. Standard 00 buckshot for situations where the contract did not say alive. Rubber slug moon clips for situations where the contract did say alive and the target needs to be discouraged from staying upright. Electric-bola moon clips — Torii's TSS-3-pattern compatible load, two trailing leads with an inductive payload — for armored or heavily-augmented targets where the priority is incapacitation through the chrome. He carries less common loads too. He does not advertise which.

The barrel is cut to the GLMZ compact firearm legal minimum. The cylinder spins reliably one-handed, which is the entire point: Silence stays in the other hand. Reloading is a moon-clip swap — old clip out under gravity once the cylinder's open, new clip in, snap closed. Six seconds with practice. Three seconds if Kyle is bleeding. The chamber and feed faces are factory-treated for adverse conditions; blood, rain, the kind of cold where steel sticks to skin.

The name Chorus was Kyle's. The katana is Silence. The shotgun is what follows Silence when Silence was not enough. Five shells in the cylinder is five chances to discover you should have planned better.
tier_availability: Tier 3 — commercial production. Available by order through Torii Security Group licensed distributors. Bird's-head grip and revolver-action configuration are factory options on the TSS-3 platform.
legality: Legal — GLMZ compact firearm classification. Requires Tier 2 commercial arms license, available to corporate employees and licensed contractors. Specialty load types (electric bola, certain inductive loads) require separate per-load endorsements that Kyle obtained through Sable's network and does not display in public.
base_technologies: Five-chamber revolver action — single-action / double-action selectable trigger
specifications: caliber: 12-gauge | capacity: 5 rounds in cylinder | effective range: contact to 15 meters (load-dependent) | barrel length: 360mm (legal minimum) | overall length: 480mm | weight: 2.1kg unloaded | action: five-chamber revolver, single-action / double-action selectable | reload: moon-clip swap (~3-6 second cycle with practice) | grip: bird's-head configuration, no stock, sharply recurved | finish: matte black ceramic-composite chassis, dark steel cylinder and action, red-line crosshatch grip texture | load compatibility: standard 12-gauge buckshot, slug, flechette; specialty TSS-3-pattern moon-clip loads including electric bola, rubber slug, inductive disruption, signal flare
tactical_use:
Close-quarters companion to the katana. Designed for one-hand operation so Silence stays in the other hand. The cylinder is selected for fights where Kyle is committing to a small budget of shots — five — and load-mixing matters more than fire rate.

Load doctrine: Kyle pre-loads moon clips by mission. A retrieval contract might be three rubber slugs followed by two buckshot — discouragement first, lethal authorization second, in case the target's friends arrive. A 'discourage but do not kill' contract is five rubber. A 'recover augmented asset without damaging the augmentation' contract is five electric-bola. Kyle does not mix load types within a single moon clip — sequence and intent are what the cylinder is for.

Firing rate is whatever the trigger pull allows. Reload speed is slow by combat standards. Kyle treats every Chorus shot as a budgeted decision; if he is firing fast enough that reload matters, he has already lost the planning round of the fight.
cultural_context:
The shotgun occupies a specific philosophical position in Kyle's loadout. The katana is his identity, his discipline, the thing he chose. The shotgun is an admission — that there are situations the blade cannot solve, that sometimes the elegant answer is not available, that the world does not arrange itself around the weapon you prefer. That Kyle carries it at all says something about how seriously he has learned to take being alive.

The revolver configuration is its own kind of confession. Five rounds, slow reload, no magazine — this is not a weapon optimized for sustained combat. It is a weapon optimized for the fight Kyle expects to have, which is short, close, and pre-decided. If he needs the sixth shot he has miscounted, and miscounting is a planning failure, not a hardware problem.

Laugh or you'd cry: the only thing more obviously antique than carrying a sword in 2225 is carrying a revolver shotgun next to it. Kyle's loadout looks, on paper, like a museum exhibit. The street has not yet developed a working theory for why the antique-looking man keeps walking home and the chrome-laden men keep not. Two competing essays on the subject exist; neither author is currently breathing.
story_hooks: Someone breaks into The Pivot and finds the TSS-3 in a locked case — Chorus engraved in small letters on the cylinder face. They know immediately whose place this is, and that whoever lives here was prepared for situations a katana cannot handle. They put it back.

Kyle fires Chorus for the first time in a year. One shot. The cylinder rotates and locks; the sound of the hammer falling is unmistakable in the enclosed space where the fight happens. Everyone who hears it knows something went wrong enough that the blade was not the answer.

Torii Security Group's armorer knows exactly who owns this unit, what moon-clip loads they have endorsements for, and that the endorsements were not obtained through proper channels. They have been watching for a long time. They have not yet decided what to do about it.
street_price: Φ 3,400 base model; Φ 4,200 with bird's-head grip option and adverse-condition chamber treatment. Specialty moon-clip loads priced per case.

physical_description.visual_profile: Compact and undecorated. Matte black ceramic-composite chassis with no stock — the bird's-head grip curves sharply backward under the receiver, giving the weapon a silhouette closer to an oversized revolver than a shotgun. The cylinder is visible from the side — five chambers, each clearly a 12-gauge bore. The Torii red-line grip texture runs along the bird's-head curve. At first glance it reads as a sidearm until you see what the cylinder is loaded with.
physical_description.weight_description: 2.1kg unloaded. Heavy enough to feel real, light enough not to remind you it's there. Loaded with five 12-gauge moon clip, it gains weight you notice on the draw.
physical_description.primary_material: Ceramic-composite chassis over steel action and cylinder. Same material specification family as the TSK-1 katana components — visual consistency was a Torii design choice.
physical_description.finish: Matte black throughout. No reflective surfaces. Red accent line in grip crosshatch texture — the only color.
physical_description.color_scheme: Black with red accent. Minimal. Intentional.
physical_description.grip_texture: Bird's-head configuration — sharply recurved grip without stock. Hand sits below and behind the bore rather than directly behind it; recoil travels up the wrist rather than rotating the muzzle. Torii red-line crosshatch texture on the full grip surface.
distinctive_features: Bird's-head grip — no stock, sharply recurved, sidearm-profile silhouette
Five-chamber cylinder visible from the side — load type identifiable by eye if the moon clip is exposed
Red-line Torii crosshatch texture on bird's-head grip
Chorus milled into the cylinder face in small clean lettering
480mm total length — conceals under a standard coat
Chamber and feed faces treated for adverse conditions including blood-slick
Cylinder release tuned for reliable one-hand operation
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: Small TSG logo on receiver. 'TSS-3' designation on the barrel rib. 'Chorus' milled into the cylinder face.
physical_description.condition_typical: Well-maintained. Cylinder action smooth, no end-shake. Kyle cleans it after every use — the moon-clip extraction depends on the cylinder staying clean.
